A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same layer-grouped SAE research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and figures, tables, equations, and renamed or relocated material support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Pythia-160M experiments covering reconstruction, feature similarity, three causal downstream tasks, and human interpretability.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on three Pythia sizes, including reconstruction, next-token prediction, automated interpretability, computational comparisons, and feature analyses.

M1.justification: Complete-linkage clustering using angular distance is retained, but v2 introduces AMAD-based selection of the smallest group count below a 0.2 distance threshold. Training also changes from v1's JumpReLU and squared-error-plus-L1 objective to TopK activation with FVU reconstruction and an auxiliary dead-latent loss (v2 Section 4.1 and Appendix B). These change the procedure beyond its Group-SAE renaming.

E1.justification: The Pile remains the underlying corpus, but v1's Indirect Object Identification, Greater Than, and Subject-Verb Agreement evaluations disappear, including their appendix results. v2 retains Pile-based reconstruction and next-token evaluation, substantially narrowing coverage of distinct causal tasks. The additional Pythia sizes are model configurations, rather than new datasets.

E2.justification: Alongside individual per-layer SAEs, v2 evaluates two new efficiency comparators: Group SAEs with evenly spaced groups and smaller SAEs trained on every layer. Table 1 compares these at reportedly matched computational cost; v1 contains neither comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds Pythia-410M and Pythia-1B configurations and broader group-count sweeps. Expansion increases from 8 to 16, angular-distance sampling from 5M to 10M tokens, and normalization, batch sizes, and optimizer settings change. Evaluation shifts to FVU and relative cross-entropy increase; Gemini detection/fuzzing on 64 features per SAE replaces human scoring of 96 sampled features. Appendix E also reverses MMCS matching from group-to-baseline to baseline-to-group.

E4.justification: v2 adds AMAD/compute versus quality analyses, expands MMCS comparisons to baseline layers against different groups, and introduces feature-activation distributions across layers in Appendix F. v1's feature-ablation tests of sufficiency and necessity, Attribution Patching/Integrated Gradients analyses, and detailed per-layer reconstruction/sparsity plots are removed. The supplementary analyses therefore change substantially.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages without uncertainty estimates. v2 Section 4.1 specifies layer-weighted means and standard deviations, and Figure 2 identifies shading as one standard deviation. This adds descriptive variability reporting, without establishing repeated training runs, seed variation, or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: The earlier causal-task and human scores are replaced by extensive new results under changed training and evaluation settings. v2 Table 2 reports 42.5%, 53.3%, and 53.7% computational savings. Table 1 reports Pythia-160M cross-entropy increases of 6.01% for AMAD grouping, 7.37% for smaller SAEs, and 5.40% for evenly spaced grouping, documenting an exception to AMAD superiority. These are new comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v2 adds AMAD's mathematical definition and threshold-selection rule, plus elementary FLOP accounting that includes activation caching. v1's indirect-effect and approximation formulations are removed. These change the formal definitions and derivations without introducing theoretical guarantees. v2 also leaves an inconsistency between the squared-error FVU definition in Equation 6 and the unsquared Frobenius-norm ratio in Equation 9.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes up to 6x training speedup, preserved causal-task performance, and human interpretability. v2 adds AMAD selection as a central contribution and claims roughly 50% computational savings, an efficiency-quality tradeoff, and superiority over compute-matched smaller SAEs. The contribution changes from demonstrating grouped training on one model to selecting groups and substantiating efficiency across three model sizes.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the AMAD turning point and layer-localized features with neighboring-layer support as explanations for effective grouping. Its limitations emphasize fixed TopK/expansion settings, Pythia/Pile-specific generalization, and restricted interpretability assessment. This replaces v1's emphasis on unresolved group-count selection, single-model scaling, and possible polysemantic interference when many layers share an SAE.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the release-upon-acceptance promise with a reported code/SAE release and access link. Appendices A–B disclose random layer sampling, detailed auxiliary-loss settings, normalization, software libraries, eight AMD MI250X GPUs, and an approximately 24-hour longest run. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although the inconsistent FVU formulas leave some implementation ambiguity.

R1.justification: The new Shared SAEs subsection discusses Yun et al., Lawson et al., and Lindsey et al.'s crosscoders, explicitly positioning Group-SAE against earlier multilayer representation methods through its efficiency-performance tradeoff. v2 also adds mechanistic-interpretability challenges and automated-interpretation literature, while removing much of v1's causal-task evaluation positioning. This is a substantive revision beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, background, and experimental narrative around Group-SAE and three research questions. Separate reconstruction, downstream-task, and human-evaluation sections become a consolidated experimental section. The appendices are reorganized into training, grouping, automated interpretation, feature similarity, and feature distribution, with retained material matched across these moves.

P2.justification: The single-column ICLR presentation becomes a two-column main text, and the method illustration is redrawn. Average bars and causal-task curves are replaced by AMAD/compute tradeoff plots with uncertainty shading, new comparison and cost tables, and automated-interpretability plots. Appendices add feature-distribution heatmaps and redesigned similarity plots; these are substantial display changes.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked a group-count selection rule and evaluated efficiency without compute-matched alternatives. v2 supplies an operational AMAD rule, caching-inclusive cost accounting, and reported matched-cost comparisons across three Pythia sizes, substantially strengthening the central efficiency argument. Expanded implementation details and release information also improve reproducibility. Removing causal-task tests and human judgments weakens direct interpretability validation, and the FVU formula inconsistency limits clarity. Nevertheless, the gains in method selection and controlled efficiency evidence constitute a substantial net improvement.
